title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 7: Independence and Integrity of the Philippine Judiciary
keywords: Independence and Integrity of the Philippine Judiciary
rule of law -- not of men
protection and enforcement of constitutional rights
weakest of the three great branches
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- an address to the XIX Biennial LAWASIA Conference in the Gold Coast, Queensland, explaining to a foreign legal audience how the integrity and independence of the Philippine judiciary are structurally upheld.

A ten-point enumeration of the constitutional guarantees that secure judicial independence, from the post-1986 rebalancing of the three branches and the grave-abuse-of-discretion mandate through security of tenure, limited presidential appointing power, fiscal autonomy, control of the bar and rule-making power.

The argument that the Court's duty to nullify gravely abusive acts is a duty rather than a power -- and that exercising it does not make the Court superior to Congress or the President but only vindicates the supremacy of the Constitution.

The closing thesis on the true source of judicial power: the judiciary remains the weakest branch, and its very weakness becomes its strength through moral courage, competence, independence and integrity expressed in well-reasoned decisions.
sub_topics: CJP thanks chairperson Chief Justice David K. Malcolm for the invitation and frames the topic as how integrity and independence are upheld in the Philippines.

He notes that although decisions are not made on the basis of what is popular or newsworthy, the judiciary must continuously retain the trust and confidence of litigants and the public -- one reason the Court ranks annually among the country's top five most credible institutions.

First, the 1987 Constitution, crafted after the 1986 bloodless People Power Revolution toppled a dictatorship, reduced executive and legislative powers and intensified judicial power; there is only one Supreme Court and no office can review its decisions.

Second, beyond correcting lower-court error, the Court is uniquely mandated to nullify any act of any branch or official, including the President or Congress, done with grave abuse of discretion -- a duty that cannot be evaded.

He lists what has been struck down under that duty: laws of Congress, executive orders, decisions of cabinet secretaries, bureau directors and top military and police officers, government contracts, and even a congressional impeachment of the Chief Justice barred by a constitutional time-bar provision.

He defines grave abuse of discretion as acting contrary to the Constitution, laws or jurisprudence, or acting whimsically or arbitrarily so patently and grossly as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty.

Third, the Court sitting en banc is sole judge of contests over the election, returns and qualifications of the President and Vice-President, with an election protest against the incumbent Vice-President still pending.
Fourth, any citizen may ask the Court to inquire into the sufficiency of the factual basis of a martial law proclamation or suspension of the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus.
Fifth, Congress is barred from enacting laws that lessen the Court's jurisdiction, and must first secure the Court's advice and concurrence to increase its appellate jurisdiction.

Sixth, judges enjoy security of tenure until 70 on good behavior, may be disciplined or removed only by the Supreme Court and only for cause, and their terms cannot be extended; SC members may be removed only by impeachment.

Seventh, the President may appoint only from a list of at least three nominees of the Judicial and Bar Council, chaired by the Chief Justice, and -- unlike in the US -- no legislative confirmation is required.

Eighth, fiscal autonomy is guaranteed twice over: judicial salaries cannot be decreased during a term, and the judiciary's appropriation cannot be cut below the previous year's and must be automatically and regularly released.

Ninth, the Court controls admission to the practice of law, conducts the bar examinations, may discipline, suspend or disbar lawyers, and has required all attorneys to join the Integrated Bar of the Philippines.

Tenth, the Court promulgates the rules of procedure and evidence for all Philippine courts and may decree rules on the protection and enforcement of constitutional rights -- a quasi-legislative prerogative.
Despite these powers the judiciary is still considered the weakest branch, having neither the legislature's budget and impeachment powers nor the executive's command of the armed forces and police.

CJP concludes that in every confrontation the Court has taken courage and performed its duty, and that its true strength lies not in brute military power or political patronage but in moral courage born of competence, independence and integrity.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces an address Justice Panganiban delivered at the XIX Biennial LAWASIA Conference in the Gold Coast, Queensland, at the invitation of chairperson Chief Justice David K. Malcolm, explaining how the integrity and independence of the Philippine judiciary are upheld. Although court decisions are not made on the basis of what is popular or newsworthy, he argued, the judiciary must continuously retain the trust of litigants and the public, and the Court's annual placement among the country's five most credible institutions is owed chiefly to its repeated demonstrations of independence. He then set out ten structural guarantees. The 1987 Constitution, written after the bloodless 1986 People Power Revolution toppled a dictatorship, reduced executive and legislative power and intensified judicial power, and no office may review the Supreme Court's decisions. The Court is uniquely mandated to nullify any act of any branch or official, including the President or Congress, done with grave abuse of discretion -- which he stressed is not just a power but a duty, since a power can be relinquished but a duty cannot be evaded -- and it has voided laws, executive orders, acts of cabinet secretaries and military and police officers, government contracts, and even a congressional impeachment of the Chief Justice barred by a constitutional time-bar. Doing so, he insisted, does not make the Court superior to the political branches but ensures that law overrides the desires and caprices of officials, so that the rule of law and not of men prevails. He further described the Court's role as sole judge of presidential and vice-presidential election contests, its power to review the factual basis of martial law or suspension of habeas corpus, the bar against laws diminishing its jurisdiction, security of tenure for judges until 70, the Judicial and Bar Council's limit on presidential appointments, fiscal autonomy, control of admission and discipline of lawyers, and its rule-making power. He closed on a paradox: the judiciary is still the weakest branch, yet its very weakness -- its lack of budget and police powers -- becomes its strength, its true power lying in moral courage born of competence, independence and integrity.
